extracted.intended_audience: writers seeking literary agents / authors preparing query letters
extracted.subtask_description: Practical step‑by‑step guidance on finding agents/editors on ManuscriptWishList and Twitter (#MSWL) and on how to reference those wishes when writing query letters. Includes search techniques, saving methods, and submission‑fit checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: One‑click Smartlinks
rubrics_metrics.description: Use ManuscriptWishList.com smartlinks to automatically search for agents who represent work like yours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These smartlinks will find agents by frequently searched genres, age groups, and keywords and will update as new agent profiles are added. Note: you may need to scroll down to see search results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custom genre/agent searches
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a custom search by checking the boxes that apply (agent/editor, genre, age group) to find precise matches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example workflow: check the appropriate boxes (agent/editor, genre, age group) → hit Search → scroll down to view results. If your manuscript spans categories (e.g., biography + history), check all boxes that could apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Twitter Advanced Search with #MSWL
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform a Twitter Advanced Search using #MSWL in the hashtag field and put keywords in the 'Any of these words' field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use related words and synonyms so you don't miss tweets where agents used different phrasing. The more tweets you see, the better — many people ask for very specific things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include related words / synonyms in searches
rubrics_metrics.description: When searching, include related words in case an agent/editor used different terms to describe a similar request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For example, if writing about cats, try multiple related keywords rather than a single term to increase relevant results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save promising tweets via Twitter likes (classic approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heart/favorite tweets you like to automatically build a one‑click list of saved tweets and make agents feel good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can view your liked tweets at https://twitter.com/[your Twitter name]/likes. This is the simplest way to keep track of potential fits without copying and pasting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Save tweets via Tweetdeck collections (tech‑savvy approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Tweetdeck to save tweets into a dedicated collection for later review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create a new column for 'collection', then drag tweets into it with the four‑way arrow or click the ellipsis and choose 'Add to collection'. Recommended for users who want better organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify an agent still wants relevant material (See my latest #MSWL tweets)
rubrics_metrics.description: On each agent profile, click 'See my latest #MSWL tweets' to view their most recent wishes and confirm they still match your manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This helps ensure freshness of fit before querying. If their recent wishes no longer match, reconsider sending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check the agent's agency website for up‑to‑date submission guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Before sending, check that agent's agency website — this is the most likely place to find their current submission requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The ManuscriptWishList profile has a button linking to the agency website. Always follow the agency's stated submission process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference a #MSWL tweet in your query opening
rubrics_metrics.description: If an agent wants a project enough to ask for it on #MSWL, reference that tweet in the opening of your query letter (one line or so).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may link directly to their tweet or quote a short line. Example opener: 'I noticed your #MSWL tweet asking for witches with real human emotions. My work…' Keep it brief and factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure logical fit when citing a tweet
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not make large logical leaps when citing a tweet; only reference a wish if it clearly applies to your manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agent asked for a nonfiction book about 17th‑century tulip mania, do not cite that tweet when pitching a contemporary novel that only mentions a tulip bouquet. If included, add a short (one line) explanation of why you think it's a fit. Some agents request this explicitly.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to handle old #MSWL tweets
rubrics_metrics.description: An older #MSWL tweet (e.g., a year old) can still be worth referencing; wishes generally do not expire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The market can change, so older wishes may be less likely to be current, but it's usually still worth sending if the wish appears applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citing editor #MSWL tweets vs agent tweets
rubrics_metrics.description: An editor's #MSWL tweet can be useful in pitching to agents, but treat editor wishes differently because editors often accept only agented submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you mention an editor's tweet in a query, be sure it's clearly applicable, and understand that editors at Big Five houses usually accept only agented submissions. An editor's wish can pique agent interest, but do not assume you can submit directly to an editor unless their website explicitly allows unagented submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm editors accept unagented submissions before sending
rubrics_metrics.description: Before submitting directly to an editor (based on an editor's #MSWL tweet), verify on their website that they accept unagented submissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many editors only accept submissions via agents; some smaller presses/editors do accept unagented submissions. The agency or publisher website will usually specify this in Submission Guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical example wording for query inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a concise, clear sentence in your query to reference the #MSWL wish and then segue into your pitch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: 'Dear Ms. Robinson, I noticed your #MSWL tweet asking for witches with real human emotions. My work…[rest of query letter]'. Keep the cited bit short and ensure the rest of the query demonstrates fit.
